title: What If It Rains Blood for 7 Days Straight?
topic: A hypothetical week of blood rain, built on real science and real disasters.

scenes.notes: Apartment at dawn, gentle rain. Maya walks in, sleepy.
scenes.narration: Tomorrow morning, you wake up to the sound of rain. Normal, gentle rain.

scenes.notes: Curtains slide open on 'curtains' → red streaks on the glass.
scenes.narration: But when you pull back the curtains, the window is streaked with red.

scenes.notes: Street at dawn: red rain, dark glossy puddles spreading.
scenes.narration: The puddles in the street are dark and glossy.

scenes.notes: Maya at the window; scent wisps drift in; she wrinkles her nose.
scenes.narration: And the air smells… like metal.

scenes.notes: Three hits: PAINT ✗, DUST ✗, then a giant blood drop slams down.
scenes.narration: It isn't paint. It isn't dust. It's blood.

scenes.notes: Earth from space; every cloud band turns red.
scenes.narration: Real blood, falling from every rain cloud on Earth.

scenes.notes: Priya the forecaster; 7 red rain icons pop in; '7 DAYS' stamp.
scenes.narration: And the forecast says it won't stop for seven days.
What would happen to our cities,
our rivers,
our farms
and our oceans?

scenes.notes: Title card with dripping letters; storm behind; music hit.
scenes.narration: To find out, we'll look at real science, real disasters, and one very strange question.

elements.text: WHAT IF IT RAINS BLOOD FOR 7 DAYS?

scenes.notes: Chapter card on parchment; timeline draws: ≈750 BC → today.
scenes.narration: People have been reporting "blood rain" for nearly three thousand years.

elements.text: Blood rain is real… sort of

scenes.notes: Zeus on a cloud raises his arm; red rain and lightning; Iliad scroll unrolls.
scenes.narration: In Homer's Iliad, Zeus sends a rain of blood as a warning of slaughter.

scenes.notes: Knights in armour march through red rain; tracking shot.
scenes.narration: In the year eleven ninety-eight, the chronicler William of Newburgh wrote that the soldiers of King Richard the Lionheart were drenched by a rain of blood.

scenes.notes: Advisers point at the sky; Richard shrugs and marches on (comic beat).
scenes.narration: Some of his advisers saw it as an evil omen. Richard ignored it.

scenes.notes: Scholar at a desk, puzzled; question marks float up; the years count on.
scenes.narration: For centuries, nobody could explain it.

scenes.notes: World map flies to India, then Kerala; red rain markers pulse.
scenes.narration: Then, in the summer of two thousand and one, red rain fell on and off for about two months over the Indian state of Kerala.

scenes.notes: Tropical night: a meteor streaks over; 'ALIEN LIFE?' newspaper spins in.
scenes.narration: Some people claimed it was alien life from a meteor.

scenes.notes: Lab: Dr. Lee at the microscope.
scenes.narration: But a study commissioned by the Indian government found a much more down-to-earth culprit:

scenes.notes: Iris into the microscope view: orange-red spores multiply.
scenes.narration: huge numbers of tiny spores from an alga called Trentepohlia.

scenes.notes: Spores shift green → orange-red.
scenes.narration: It belongs to the green algae, but it's packed with orange-red pigment.

scenes.notes: Spinning DNA; 2015 genetic study names Trentepohlia annulata.
scenes.narration: In twenty fifteen, a genetic study pinned down the exact species: Trentepohlia annulata.

scenes.notes: Map of Europe & North Africa: dust route draws from the Sahara to Britain.
scenes.narration: In Europe, "blood rain" usually has an even simpler cause.

scenes.notes: Desert: wind lifts a dust storm high; rain clouds wash it back down.
scenes.narration: Strong winds lift red dust from the Sahara Desert high into the sky, and rain washes it back down.

scenes.notes: UK street, orange-tinted rain on a dusty car; colour chips yellow ✓ orange ✓ red ✗.
scenes.narration: Britain's Met Office points out that this rain usually looks more yellow or orange than red.

scenes.notes: Checklist: water ✓ dust ✓ microbes ✓ · real blood ✗ with a big cross on the drop.
scenes.narration: So every blood rain ever investigated has turned out to be water, tinted by dust or microbes. Not one drop of real blood.

scenes.notes: Ocean under sun; vapour rises, gathers into a cloud, droplets form.
scenes.narration: And there's a good reason for that. Rain begins as water vapour, which condenses into droplets inside clouds.

scenes.notes: Cells, proteins and salts try to rise, hit an invisible ceiling and drop back.
scenes.narration: Blood is a mixture of cells, proteins and salts, and none of those can evaporate and rise into a cloud.

scenes.notes: 'PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE' stamp → lightbulb → 'THOUGHT EXPERIMENT'.
scenes.narration: Real blood rain is physically impossible. Which makes it the perfect thought experiment.

scenes.notes: Blueprint world; Dr. Lee presents; HYPOTHETICAL tag lands and stays from here on.
scenes.narration: From here on, everything is hypothetical, but we'll build it on real science. So, let's set the rules.

scenes.notes: Globe with rain bands switching from white/blue to red, same shapes. RULE 1 card.
scenes.narration: Rule 1. For seven days, everywhere it would normally rain, it rains ordinary mammalian blood instead, in exactly the same amounts.

scenes.notes: RULE 2: shield; virus ✗, skull ✗, then a clean drop ✓.
scenes.narration: Rule 2. The blood is clean when it leaves the clouds. No diseases, no poisons, just blood.

scenes.notes: Rain cloud; counter rolls to 500,000 km³ per year.
scenes.narration: So, how much are we talking about? Scientists estimate that around half a million cubic kilometers of rain and snow fall on Earth every year.

scenes.notes: A 7-day calendar tears through; counter drops to 10,000 km³.
scenes.narration: Seven days of that is roughly 10,000 cubic kilometers.

scenes.notes: One person (5 L) → camera pulls back as the crowd fills to billions → all of it is one small cube < 0.05 km³.
scenes.narration: An adult human holds about five liters of blood. Add up every person alive, and it comes to less than a 20th of a single cubic kilometer.

scenes.notes: Tiny human-blood cube vs a giant crimson cube growing to true scale (58× edge = 200,000× volume); camera tilts up.
scenes.narration: That means our seven-day storm would drop more than 200,000 times as much blood as there is in the entire human race.

elements.text: the blood of the entire human race (to scale)

scenes.notes: Pie: ocean ¾ / land ¼; '2,000+ km³ lands on us'.
scenes.narration: About three-quarters of it would fall into the ocean. The rest, more than 2,000 cubic kilometers, lands on us.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 1; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day 1.

scenes.notes: City street, red rain; people under umbrellas look up, surprised.
scenes.narration: The first thing people notice is the color.

scenes.notes: Microscope: pale-yellow plasma with tumbling red cells; 55% / 45% labels.
scenes.narration: Blood is about 55% plasma, a pale yellow liquid that's mostly water, and about 45% red blood cells.

scenes.notes: Deep zoom into one red cell: haemoglobin molecule with a glowing Fe atom.
scenes.narration: Those cells are packed with haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that gives blood its deep red color.

scenes.notes: Street two-shot: Maya and Alex sniff and pull faces; 'METAL?' gets ✗.
scenes.narration: The second thing people notice is the smell. That metallic scent of blood doesn't actually come from metal.

scenes.notes: Flow diagram: skin oils + blood/iron → 1-octen-3-one → nose. 2006.
scenes.narration: In 2006, chemists showed that when blood or iron touches our skin, it reacts with the oils on it to form a compound called 1-octen-3-one, and our noses are extremely sensitive to it.

scenes.notes: Wildlife park: tiger and wild dog sniff two logs — 'single chemical' = 'real blood'. 2014.
scenes.narration: Blood also carries its own signature odor molecule. In a 2014 experiment, large carnivores were just as interested in a wooden log soaked in that single chemical as in a log soaked in real blood.

scenes.notes: Scent wisps rising everywhere (quick whip panels).
scenes.narration: Now imagine that scent rising from every street,

scenes.notes: Scent wisps rising everywhere (quick whip panels).
scenes.narration: every field,

scenes.notes: Scent wisps rising everywhere (quick whip panels).
scenes.narration: and every forest at once.

scenes.notes: Forest at dusk: fox and wolf lift their noses, circle, confused (question marks).
scenes.narration: For animals that hunt by smell, the whole world would suddenly smell like wounded prey, with no prey to be found. No one can test how animals would react on a global scale, but confusion is a safe bet.

scenes.notes: Macro: a drop lands on a car bonnet, spreads, and thickens into gel; a clock spins.
scenes.narration: And then there's the third thing. Blood is sticky. Outside the body, blood normally begins to clot within minutes. Every drop that lands starts turning from liquid into gel.

scenes.notes: Evening city, glossy dark red; pull back to reveal massive storm clouds still rolling in.
scenes.narration: By the evening of day one, cars, roofs, and pavements are coated in a dark tacky film, and the storm has barely started.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 2; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day two.

scenes.notes: Street cutaway: road, gutter, drain, pipes; blue water flows fast (built for water).
scenes.narration: Our cities were built for water. Gutters, storm drains and sewers are designed to carry a thin, runny liquid away quickly.

scenes.notes: Two beakers drain side by side: water fast, blood slow; lumps form.
scenes.narration: Blood is several times thicker than water, and as it clots, it forms soft, rubbery lumps.

scenes.notes: Same cutaway, now red: clots catch at the grate, flow stops, level rises.
scenes.narration: Clots collect in drain grates and narrow pipes. Everything behind them backs up.

scenes.notes: Street level: red flood with floating clots; Maya and Sam on the front steps.
scenes.narration: In places that get heavy rain, streets would likely flood with a mix of liquid blood and floating clots.

scenes.notes: Iris into a puddle → microscope: bacteria drift in from soil and air.
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, something invisible is happening. The blood left the clouds clean, but the ground, the air, and our skin are covered in bacteria.

scenes.notes: Lab: Dr. Lee with a red-agar petri dish; colonies bloom.
scenes.narration: And to a microbe, blood is a feast. It's so nutritious that laboratories add it to a jelly called blood agar, just to grow bacteria.

scenes.notes: Bacteria split 1→2→4…; fast clock; counter shoots to 1,000,000,000+.
scenes.narration: In warm, rich conditions, some bacteria can double their numbers every 20 minutes. At that pace, a single cell could, in theory, become billions in less than half a day.

scenes.notes: Night puddle turns murky; streetlight flickers; music drop.
scenes.narration: By the end of day two, the blood in every puddle is no longer clean. And that's when the real trouble begins.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 3; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day three

scenes.notes: Hazy hot city; green-brown stink wisps; people in face masks.
scenes.narration: and the smell changes. As bacteria break down blood proteins, they release sulphur compounds and other foul gases, the same chemistry behind the stench of rotting meat.

scenes.notes: Macro fly lands by a puddle; swarm builds.
scenes.narration: To flies, that stench is a dinner bell. Research on blowflies and their relatives shows that it's the bacteria growing in blood that produce the scents that draw females in to lay their eggs.

elements.text: bacteria make the scent → flies lay eggs

scenes.notes: Line chart 'fly numbers (illustrative)' curving upward; swarm thickens.
scenes.narration: With rotting blood everywhere, fly populations could explode within days, especially in warm countries.

scenes.notes: Flow diagram: rain → river → reservoir → city taps.
scenes.narration: Then, there's drinking water. Many cities draw their water from rivers and reservoirs that are fed by rain.

scenes.notes: Treatment plant: red water fills tanks, filters clog, warning lights; Jordan closes the intake.
scenes.narration: Treatment plants are built to remove modest amounts of organic material. Not a river made largely of blood. Filters would clog, and operators would likely have to shut their intakes and rely on stored water.

scenes.notes: Supermarket shelf empties fast (time-lapse); shoppers rush.
scenes.narration: Bottled water would probably vanish from shops within hours.

scenes.notes: Alley: rats, crows and gulls feast; Maya recoils. Dutch angle.
scenes.narration: Not every creature would suffer, though. Scavengers like rats, crows, and gulls would suddenly find food everywhere, and their numbers could climb fast. For a few weeks, the winners of this disaster would be the animals we least want around us.

scenes.notes: Camera cranes up over the city…
scenes.narration: But the most dangerous changes aren't happening on the streets.

scenes.notes: …and swings to the red river beside it.
scenes.narration: They're happening in the water.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 4; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day 4

scenes.notes: River from its bank: the water turns from blue to red as runoff flows in.
scenes.narration: All that blood is flowing downhill into streams, lakes, and rivers.

scenes.notes: Underwater: bacteria multiply, O₂ bubbles wink out; label BOD.
scenes.narration: And this is where things turn deadly. When bacteria digest organic matter, they consume the oxygen dissolved in the water. Engineers measure this with something called biochemical oxygen demand.

scenes.notes: Bar chart: sewage bar tiny, cattle-blood bar shoots off the chart.
scenes.narration: Ordinary household sewage has a demand of a few hundred milligrams per liter. Cattle blood has been measured at around 150,000. That's hundreds of times more.

scenes.notes: REAL: US map → Alabama; the Mulberry Fork lights up where the pipe failed (2019).
scenes.narration: We know what happens when even a small amount of this kind of waste reaches a river. In 2019, a pipe failure at a poultry plant in Alabama sent wastewater into the Mulberry Fork of the Black Warrior River.

scenes.notes: REAL: river oxygen gauge falls; dead fish float up; counter → 175,000.
scenes.narration: As bacteria fed on it, they used up the oxygen, and an estimated 175,000 fish died.

scenes.notes: World map: major rivers light up red one after another.
scenes.narration: Now picture that in every river on the planet, at the same time.

scenes.notes: Underwater: fish, frogs and insects struggle as the gauge hits zero.
scenes.narration: Fish, insects, frogs, anything that breathes underwater would begin to suffocate.

scenes.notes: Same river as s63: alive (DAY 1) → still and murky (DAY 4).
scenes.narration: Rivers that were full of life on day one could be almost lifeless by day four.

scenes.notes: Loop diagram: dead fish → rot → more bacteria → less O₂ → more dead fish.
scenes.narration: And when the fish die, they rot too, feeding even more bacteria and stealing even more oxygen. It's a vicious circle.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 5; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day 5

scenes.notes: Farm wide pan under red rain.
scenes.narration: Out in the countryside. And here's a strange twist.

scenes.notes: REAL: Walter in his garden holds a BLOOD MEAL sack and sprinkles a pinch on a plant.
scenes.narration: Dried blood is actually sold as a fertilizer called blood meal.

scenes.notes: N 12–14% badge; leaf tips turn brown; a seedling droops.
scenes.narration: It's about 12-14% nitrogen, and gardeners are told to use it sparingly because too much nitrogen burns plants. Leaf tips turn brown and young seedlings can die.

scenes.notes: Field under heavy red rain; crop rows wilt; 'OVERDOSE'.
scenes.narration: Our storm isn't a sprinkle of fertilizer. It's days of liquid blood soaking into the soil. The likely result is an overdose.

scenes.notes: Soil cutaway: roots, O₂ fading, bacteria spreading, blood soaking down.
scenes.narration: And as that blood rots underground, bacteria use up the oxygen in the soil, oxygen that plant roots need to breathe.

scenes.notes: Cows at red troughs with flies; a CLEAN WATER truck drives in.
scenes.narration: Farm animals would face their own problems. Pastures, ponds, and water troughs would be coated in rotting blood, swarming with flies. Farmers would have to bring clean water and feed to their herds on a scale no emergency plan has ever imagined.

scenes.notes: Map: Mississippi system draws itself down to the Gulf — rivers lead to the sea.
scenes.narration: Even after the rain ends, much of that nitrogen will wash into rivers, and rivers lead to the sea.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 6; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day 6

scenes.notes: Open sea under red rain; the ¾ pie returns briefly.
scenes.narration: Remember, about three-quarters of the storm fell straight into the ocean.

scenes.notes: Pan from open sea (diluted) to the coast (concentrated).
scenes.narration: The open sea is so vast that it would dilute much of it, but coastlines, bays, and river mouths are a different story.

scenes.notes: REAL: Mississippi draws itself; farm markers along it; a green bloom spreads at the river mouth.
scenes.narration: Scientists already know what happens when rivers carry too many nutrients to the sea. Every summer, fertilizer washing off farms along the Mississippi River feeds huge blooms of algae in the Gulf of Mexico.

scenes.notes: Underwater: algae sink, oxygen vanishes, fish leave; a dark zone spreads.
scenes.narration: When the algae die and sink, bacteria break them down and use up the oxygen, creating a dead zone.

scenes.notes: REAL: Gulf map, the 2024 dead zone grows; 17,000 km²; New Jersey slides over it for scale.
scenes.narration: In 2024, that dead zone covered about 17,000 square kilometers, roughly the size of the U.S. state of New Jersey.

scenes.notes: HYPOTHETICAL: world map, dark patches appear along coastlines everywhere.
scenes.narration: Our blood storm would deliver a nutrient load to coastal waters on a scale never seen before. Dead zones could appear along coastlines all over the world at the same time.

scenes.notes: Day card: calendar tears to DAY 7; thunder.
scenes.narration: Day 7.

scenes.notes: Last drops fall, clouds break, light rays stream in; tilt up.
scenes.narration: And finally, the rain stops.

scenes.notes: Rust-coloured street; puddles dry into brown crust; Maya steps outside.
scenes.narration: The sun comes out on a world painted the colour of rust. On roads and roofs, the remaining blood dries into a brown, flaky crust.

scenes.notes: Jordan's crew with hoses; a tanker spraying; the clean-water gauge drains.
scenes.narration: Cleaning it up would take months of fire hoses, street sweepers and enormous amounts of clean water, the one thing that's suddenly in short supply.

scenes.notes: Time-lapse river: clean rain, water fades brown-red → blue, fish swim back, life returns.
scenes.narration: Nature would recover, but slowly. Normal rain would gradually flush the rivers clean. Fish would return from waters that escaped the worst. Plants would regrow.

scenes.notes: Timeline of years 1 → 2 → 3 → ? over the recovering river.
scenes.narration: Still, after the Alabama spill alone, officials warned that the river could take years to fully recover. After a storm like this, some ecosystems might take far longer.

scenes.notes: Front page 'THE WEEK IT RAINED BLOOD' spins in; Maya and Sam at the window.
scenes.narration: The week itself would be remembered as one of the strangest and most frightening events in human history.

scenes.notes: Rewind back to reality.
scenes.narration: Of course, this will never happen.

scenes.notes: Clouds only make rain from vapour; real blood rain = desert dust or algae spores.
scenes.narration: Clouds can only make rain from water vapour, and every real "blood rain" ever investigated has been water, coloured by desert dust or tiny algae.

scenes.notes: Globe with a glowing water-cycle loop around it.
scenes.narration: But the thought experiment reveals something real. Earth's water cycle moves an astonishing amount of material, quietly, every single day.

scenes.notes: REAL: farm & factory runoff → rivers → oceans → dead zones; O₂ gauge drops (callback).
scenes.narration: And many of the disasters in our story already happen in the real world, just on a smaller scale. When waste and fertiliser wash into rivers and oceans, they steal the oxygen that life depends on.

scenes.notes: Park in light clear rain: Sam splashes in a puddle, Maya smiles, sunlight breaks through.
scenes.narration: So the next time it rains, take a moment to appreciate it. Clear, clean water, falling from the sky, keeping the whole planet alive.

scenes.notes: Clear puddle reflecting the sky; the title returns; end card.
scenes.narration: And maybe… be glad it's just water.

elements.text: WHAT IF IT RAINS BLOOD FOR 7 DAYS?
